(only scanned letter-spacing differs). The second half of the quote, sec. 8.7 printed pp. 210-211 (PDF 234-235), is also verbatim: '..those dialects (But,…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Kamayo retains the Proto-Central-Philippine contrastive (lexical) word accent of the Bisayan/Tagalog type: accent falls unpredictably on the penult (realised as a long stressed open penult) or on the ultima, per lexeme (sec. 8.10: PBS *púnuq 'tree trunk' vs *punúq 'full'); in that system a closed penult is regularly stressed; additionally Kamayo has phonemically long final vowels from compensatory lengthening after loss of *-l- (qabo 'ashes' vs qabo: 'smoke'). Zorc 1993 (Table 2, class C) and Zorc 1978 (p. 72, Group C) restate this classification.
new_statements.exceptions: Long final vowels (compensatory, after *-l- loss) are an extra contrast on the ultima; the statement is hedged as 'generally preserves' and attributes retention to contact with accent-preserving South Bisayan neighbours. No synchronic rule list for Kamayo itself is given; the closed-penult rule is stated for Bisayan dialects (sec. 8.10.2) and only implied for Kamayo.
new_statements.domain_note: Comparative/historical statement about the word (lexical citation forms with accent marks, e.g. Kamayo hatág, qi-tún, kudíng in the etyma lists); Zorc 1978:72 adds that in all Philippine languages stress/pitch accent is also an accent-group (phrase) feature that can be overridden by intonation, with vowel length the primary word-level cue.
new_statements.identity_note: Zorc's 'Kamayo (NMk)' = Kamayo of Surigao del Sur, northern dialects Marihatag-Hinatuan and southern dialects Bislig-Lingig (PL-C44 Table 3 no. 15), i.e. the same variety as Glottolog kama1363 / ISO kyk (Zorc classes it as North Mansakan; Lobel 2013 as Dabawenyo). Schmitt 2022's data are from Bislig speakers. The statement is comparative (retention of Proto-Central-Philippine contrastive accent), not a synchronic phonological description; no modern first-hand phonology of Kamayo with a stress section was found — the only modern grammar sketch (Schmitt 2022) has no phonology chapter.
